data.hypothesis: The selected parent uses subtraction to form two-bit population counts. Replacing only that first SWAR stage with masked addition tests whether add-based field aggregation performs better under the frozen compiler; the extra mask/add work may instead make it slower. The remaining count stages and serial recurrence are unchanged. This is distinct from the measured multiply-reduction and nibble-subtraction variants, whose results show that SWAR formulations need measurement rather than presumed ranking.

memory_lessons.applicability: Compare isolated popcount formulations under the same frozen protocol; do not infer that a change will combine well with other variants.
memory_lessons.claim: The supplied measurements differ substantially across valid SWAR candidates: 53f75ac2fb994a31 measured 0.435 ms, 7de0b21fee3a4a9d measured 0.0817 ms, and 65338540dbde43de and e378502f29694326 measured 0.391 ms and 0.408 ms. These results establish differing observed outcomes, not the cause of the differences or a general ranking.
memory_lessons.next_experiment: Measure this candidate with the frozen build and official protocol, then compare its result with the selected parent without attributing any difference beyond what the isolated change supports.

data.notes: The pairwise masked addition stores each pair's bit count (0–2) in its two-bit field; the following stages produce nibble counts (0–4), byte counts (0–8), and a total no greater than 32. This gives exact counts for every uint32_t input, with the final 0x3f mask retaining the total. The ordered recurrence, uint32_t accumulation and wraparound, dimensions, output overwrite, and thread usage are unchanged. No exhaustive runtime enumeration or official measurement was performed here; the controller should run its correctness and performance protocol.
transformations: Replaced the subtraction-based two-bit SWAR population-count stage with masked addition of the even- and odd-position bits.
Kept the remaining SWAR stages and preserved the ordered uint32_t recurrence, generic dimensions, output overwrite, and existing thread usage.
